headline: Microsoft launches new in-house AI models cutting costs up to 89% vs. OpenAI
summary: Microsoft AI introduces MAI-Image-2.5-Pro for premium image generation and MAI-Voice-2-Flash for high-volume speech, showcasing significant cost reductions and in-house capabilities.
details: Microsoft AI has released two new in-house models: MAI-Image-2.5-Pro, its highest-fidelity image generator, and MAI-Voice-2-Flash, a speech model for high-volume enterprise workloads. The company reports these models cut costs by up to 89% compared to using OpenAI's models.

This move signals Microsoft's aggressive strategy to power its own products without relying on third-party frontier models. These homegrown AI solutions are now production infrastructure, serving millions of users across Bing, PowerPoint, OneDrive, Dynamics 365, Excel, GitHub Copilot, and Azure.

MAI-Image-2.5-Pro targets premium image generation, offering detailed editing and precise in-image text rendering, a common weak spot for AI image models. It is priced at $5 per million text input tokens, $8 per million image input tokens, and $106 per million image output tokens.

MAI-Voice-2-Flash focuses on speed and cost-efficiency, running twice as fast as its predecessor and costing 32% less at $15 per million characters. It is designed for high-volume applications like call centers and real-time speech, where latency and cost are critical.

Deployment metrics show Bing Image Creator now runs entirely on MAI-Image-2.5. In PowerPoint, this model reduces GPU costs by up to 84% compared to OpenAI's GPT-Image-2. OneDrive also sees a 26% increase in save rates and 2.5 times greater efficiency.
MAI-Voice-2-Flash powers Dynamics 365 Contact Center, achieving GPU cost reductions of up to 89%. It's also integrated into Azure Voice Live for developers building speech-to-speech agents.

In healthcare, Dragon Copilot, used by 170,000 medical providers, now uses MAI-Transcribe-1.5 for multilingual workflows across 58 languages. Internal evaluations show a 50% relative reduction in transcription and language-identification error rates, crucial for clinical notes.

headline_marked: [[Namecheap gave account to unverified third party]] after simple phone request, user reports
headline: Namecheap gave account to unverified third party after simple phone request, user reports
summary: A user's domain registrar account was compromised after Namecheap changed password and email for an unverified caller, highlighting a critical security flaw.
details: A Namecheap user reported that their domain registrar account was handed over to an unverified third party. The new club leader, who needed access to a club domain, convinced Namecheap support to change the account's password and email address without any verification from the original owner.

The original account holder, who was the registered owner of the domain, was not contacted or verified during this process. Namecheap made these changes simply based on a phone call from the third party, despite having the ability to contact the actual account owner.

The user described this as a 'massive vulnerability,' noting that Namecheap had previously called them for verification on a different support ticket. They emphasized that this was not even social engineering, but a fundamental flaw in Namecheap's account security protocols.

As a result of this incident, the user has already moved a dozen of their most critical domains away from Namecheap. They warn that it appears to be alarmingly easy for a third party to take over a Namecheap account by simply 'asking nicely'.
